theme: Justice, integrity, and the king’s heart in the LORD’s hand
readingInstruction: Read Proverbs 20:1-21:31. These chapters continue the collection. Notice what is said about the king, justice, and the heart, and the great statement in 21:1 and 21:31.
settingTheScene: The sayings of chapters 20 and 21 have a strong focus on rulers, justice, and honest dealing. This is fitting for a collection associated with a king. They also continue the theme of God’s rule over human hearts and plans. As the last of the Solomonic sayings before the “Sayings of the Wise,” these chapters are a high point in the theology of providence.
observation: “Wine is a mocker, strong drink a brawler, and whoever is led astray by it is not wise” (20:1).
“Who can say, I have made my heart pure; I am clean from my sin?” (20:9).
“The hearing ear and the seeing eye, the LORD has made them both” (20:12).
“Do not say, I will repay evil; wait for the LORD, and he will deliver you” (20:22).
“The king’s heart is a stream of water in the hand of the LORD; he turns it wherever he will” (21:1).
“Every way of a man is right in his own eyes, but the LORD weighs the heart” (21:2).
“To do righteousness and justice is more acceptable to the LORD than sacrifice” (21:3).
“The horse is made ready for the day of battle, but the victory belongs to the LORD” (21:31).
interpretation:
Chapter 20 begins with a warning about drink, then turns to honesty and the king’s role. A king who sits on the throne of judgment “winnows all evil with his eyes.” Good rule requires moral discernment. Yet the chapter also contains a question that humbles every ruler: “Who can say, I have made my heart pure; I am clean from my sin?” The answer is no one. Even the wisest king, and even the wisest reader, needs forgiveness.

Verse 22 is a gem for those who are wronged: “Do not say, I will repay evil; wait for the LORD, and he will deliver you.” It echoes the principle of David’s restraint with Saul. Vengeance belongs to God. Waiting is an act of faith. Honest scales and weights also come up repeatedly. “Unequal weights and unequal measures are both alike an abomination to the LORD.” The God of the temple cares about the marketplace.

Chapter 21 opens with one of the most sweeping statements of God’s sovereignty. “The king’s heart is a stream of water in the hand of the LORD; he turns it wherever he will.” The most powerful person in the land has a heart that is directed by God, as a farmer directs the channel of irrigation. God is not threatened by kings. He guides them, even when they do not know it. This is comfort for those living under unjust or foolish rulers.

Verse 3 repeats what Samuel told Saul and the prophets will say: “To do righteousness and justice is more acceptable to the LORD than sacrifice.” Ritual without righteousness is empty. And verse 13 states a principle of mercy: “Whoever closes his ear to the cry of the poor will himself call out and not be answered.”

The chapter ends with a verse that sums up providence: “The horse is made ready for the day of battle, but the victory belongs to the LORD.” Prepare, plan, and work, but know that the result is God’s. The following verse, 21:30, says, “No wisdom, no understanding, no counsel can avail against the LORD.”
connection: Paul says that governing authorities are instituted by God (Romans 13:1), and 1 Timothy 2:1-2 urges prayer for kings. Jesus said, “My Father is working until now, and I am working” (John 5:17). Romans 12:19 echoes verse 22: “Never avenge yourselves… leave it to the wrath of God.” Jesus quoted the prophets that God desires “mercy, and not sacrifice” (Matthew 9:13). Psalm 33:16-17 adds that a war horse is a false hope for victory.
application:
Pray for a leader whose decisions affect you, trusting that God can turn their heart.

When you are wronged, practice waiting on the LORD instead of repaying.

Do your part in a hard task, and release the outcome to God.
prayerPrompts: Admit before God that you cannot make your own heart pure.
Ask him for mercy and for patience when you are wronged.
Thank him that he holds even the king’s heart.
